name: Interscalene Brachial Plexus Block
targetNervesOrPlane: Brachial plexus roots/trunks (C5–C7 predominant; C8/T1 often spared)
commonIndications: Shoulder surgery
Proximal humerus surgery
patientPosition: Supine or semi-sitting, head turned away from the side to be blocked
landmarkTechnique: Classic landmark approach identifies the interscalene groove between anterior and middle scalene muscles at the level of the cricoid cartilage (C6), with a nerve stimulator confirming a motor response before injection — largely superseded by ultrasound guidance where available.
ultrasoundApproach: Probe placed transversely at the level of the cricoid cartilage lateral to the sternocleidomastoid; the plexus roots/trunks typically appear as a column of hypoechoic round structures ("stoplight sign") between anterior and middle scalene muscles.
needleApproach: In-plane, lateral-to-medial, targeting the space between the visualized trunks.
keyComplications: Phrenic nerve palsy / hemidiaphragmatic paresis (very common, often near-universal without dose reduction)
Horner's syndrome (ipsilateral ptosis/miosis/anhidrosis)
Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement (hoarseness)
Inadvertent intrathecal/epidural spread
Vertebral artery injection
contraindications: Severe respiratory disease intolerant of hemidiaphragmatic paresis
pearls: Counsel patients pre-block about expected transient hoarseness/ptosis and hand weakness/numbness
Consider lower-volume or superior-trunk-only technique to reduce phrenic nerve involvement, per unit practice
Poor block for hand/ulnar-distribution surgery — inferior trunk (C8/T1) is often spared

source.title: Widely-taught regional anesthesia technique structure (textbook-level, ASRA/NYSORA-style teaching descriptions)

name: Supraclavicular Brachial Plexus Block
commonIndications: Elbow, forearm, and hand surgery
Sometimes called the "spinal of the arm" for its dense, reliable block
patientPosition: Supine, head turned slightly away from the side to be blocked
landmarkTechnique: Historically performed with surface landmarks (midpoint of clavicle) and nerve stimulation; carries a higher classically-taught pneumothorax risk without direct visualization, which is why ultrasound guidance is now standard practice.
ultrasoundApproach: Probe placed in the supraclavicular fossa in the coronal-oblique plane; the plexus is visualized as a cluster of hypoechoic nodules ("bunch of grapes") lateral and superficial to the subclavian artery, with the first rib and pleura visible deep to the plexus.
needleApproach: In-plane, lateral-to-medial, targeting the "corner pocket" between the artery and first rib for dense block.
keyComplications: Pneumothorax (classic concern, reduced with real-time ultrasound visualization)
Phrenic nerve palsy (less frequent than interscalene but still occurs)
Vascular puncture (subclavian artery is immediately adjacent)
pearls: Often considered the most reliable single-injection block for the entire arm distal to the shoulder
Keep the needle tip visualized at all times given pleural proximity
Confirm no intravascular injection with intermittent aspiration and slow incremental injection

source.title: Widely-taught regional anesthesia technique structure (textbook-level, ASRA/NYSORA-style teaching descriptions)

name: Infraclavicular Brachial Plexus Block
targetNervesOrPlane: Brachial plexus cords (lateral, posterior, medial) around the axillary artery
commonIndications: Elbow, forearm, and hand surgery
Favorable for continuous catheter placement (stable landmarks, less catheter migration with arm movement)
patientPosition: Supine, arm adducted at the side or abducted to 90°
landmarkTechnique: Classic coracoid approach uses the coracoid process as a surface landmark with a nerve-stimulator-guided needle insertion inferomedial to it; largely replaced by ultrasound guidance.
ultrasoundApproach: Parasagittal probe placement just medial/inferior to the coracoid process; the axillary artery is visualized with the three cords typically seen clustered around it (lateral cord superficial/lateral, posterior cord deep, medial cord between artery and vein).
needleApproach: In-plane, cephalad-to-caudad, aiming to deposit local anesthetic posterior to the artery (the "U-shape" spread target) for circumferential coverage of all three cords.
keyComplications: Vascular puncture (axillary artery/vein)
Pneumothorax (lower risk than supraclavicular but still possible)
Incomplete block if a cord is missed
pearls: Good choice for continuous perineural catheter techniques given the fixed, deep location relative to the shoulder
Posterior cord is often the last to block — deposit local anesthetic posterior to the artery first

source.title: Widely-taught regional anesthesia technique structure (textbook-level, ASRA/NYSORA-style teaching descriptions)

name: Axillary Brachial Plexus Block
targetNervesOrPlane: Median, ulnar, radial, and musculocutaneous nerves (terminal branches, individually identifiable around the axillary artery)
commonIndications: Forearm and hand surgery
Favored where phrenic-sparing is important (no diaphragmatic risk)
patientPosition: Supine, arm abducted to 90° and externally rotated ("surrender" position)
landmarkTechnique: Historic transarterial or nerve-stimulator technique injects around the palpated axillary artery pulse; ultrasound guidance now allows each of the four nerves to be individually visualized and blocked.
ultrasoundApproach: Probe placed transversely in the axilla; median, ulnar, and radial nerves are visualized as discrete hyperechoic structures around the axillary artery, with the musculocutaneous nerve typically seen separately within or between the coracobrachialis/biceps muscles.
needleApproach: In-plane, targeting each of the four nerves individually with small aliquots of local anesthetic around each (rather than a single large-volume injection).
localAnestheticVolume: 20–35 mL total (split across the 4 target nerves)
keyComplications: Vascular puncture (axillary artery — direct compression usually manages this)
Intravascular injection
Incomplete block if musculocutaneous nerve is missed (often blocked separately as it exits the plexus more proximally)
contraindications: Inability to abduct the arm (e.g. severe shoulder pathology)
pearls: No phrenic nerve risk — a good choice for patients with significant pulmonary disease needing forearm/hand surgery
Musculocutaneous nerve commonly requires a separate injection since it often exits the sheath proximal to the axilla

source.title: Widely-taught regional anesthesia technique structure (textbook-level, ASRA/NYSORA-style teaching descriptions)

name: Femoral Nerve Block
targetNervesOrPlane: Femoral nerve, lateral to the femoral artery within the femoral triangle
commonIndications: Anterior thigh/knee surgery
Femur fracture analgesia
Total knee arthroplasty (increasingly superseded by adductor canal block to preserve quadriceps strength)
landmarkTechnique: Classic technique palpates the femoral artery pulse just below the inguinal ligament and directs the needle lateral to it with nerve-stimulator confirmation (quadriceps twitch/patellar snap).
ultrasoundApproach: Probe placed transversely at the inguinal crease; the femoral nerve appears as a hyperechoic triangular/oval structure lateral to the femoral artery, deep to the fascia iliaca.
needleApproach: In-plane, lateral-to-medial, depositing local anesthetic around the nerve deep to the fascia iliaca.
keyComplications: Quadriceps weakness / fall risk (motor block is expected, not a complication per se, but a major safety counselling point)
Vascular puncture
Rare femoral nerve injury
pearls: Counsel every patient about quadriceps weakness and fall precautions before ambulation
Adductor canal block is increasingly preferred for knee arthroplasty analgesia specifically to preserve quadriceps strength and reduce fall risk

source.title: Widely-taught regional anesthesia technique structure (textbook-level, ASRA/NYSORA-style teaching descriptions)

name: Adductor Canal Block
targetNervesOrPlane: Saphenous nerve and articular branches within the adductor (subsartorial) canal, mid-thigh
commonIndications: Total knee arthroplasty analgesia
Anterior/medial knee and lower leg procedures where motor-sparing is desired
landmarkTechnique: Not typically performed by landmark technique alone — ultrasound guidance is standard given the depth and variability of the canal.
ultrasoundApproach: Probe placed transversely at the mid-to-distal thigh over the sartorius muscle; the canal is identified deep to sartorius, with the saphenous nerve typically seen adjacent to the femoral (superficial femoral) artery.
needleApproach: In-plane, lateral-to-medial, depositing local anesthetic around the neurovascular bundle within the canal.
keyComplications: Generally low complication rate given the predominantly sensory target
Vascular puncture (femoral vessels within canal)
pearls: Preserves quadriceps strength relative to a femoral nerve block — a major reason it has become the preferred technique for knee arthroplasty in many enhanced-recovery pathways
Provides less coverage of the anterior/lateral knee capsule than a femoral block — may need supplementation for some surgical approaches

source.title: Widely-taught regional anesthesia technique structure (textbook-level, ASRA/NYSORA-style teaching descriptions)

name: Sciatic Nerve Block (Popliteal Approach)
targetNervesOrPlane: Sciatic nerve, proximal to its bifurcation into tibial and common peroneal nerves
commonIndications: Foot and ankle surgery
Distal lower leg surgery (often combined with a saphenous/adductor canal block for medial coverage)
patientPosition: Prone, lateral, or supine with the leg elevated, depending on operator preference
landmarkTechnique: Classic technique uses surface landmarks in the popliteal fossa (apex of the popliteal triangle) with nerve-stimulator-guided needle advancement.
ultrasoundApproach: Probe placed transversely in the popliteal crease; the tibial and common peroneal components are traced proximally to their confluence into the sciatic nerve, typically seen as a hyperechoic oval structure superficial to the popliteal artery.
needleApproach: In-plane or out-of-plane, targeting a position just proximal to the bifurcation for a single injection covering both terminal branches.
onsetTime: 20–30 minutes (can be slower given nerve size)
keyComplications: Foot drop / motor block (expected effect, counsel accordingly)
Vascular puncture (popliteal vessels)
Rare nerve injury
pearls: Injecting just proximal to the sciatic bifurcation improves block reliability compared to injecting at the bifurcation itself
Combine with a saphenous/adductor canal block for procedures involving the medial ankle/foot, which the sciatic nerve does not cover

source.title: Widely-taught regional anesthesia technique structure (textbook-level, ASRA/NYSORA-style teaching descriptions)

name: Transversus Abdominis Plane (TAP) Block
targetNervesOrPlane: Anterior rami of T7–L1 (thoracolumbar nerves) within the transversus abdominis plane
commonIndications: Analgesia for lower abdominal incisions (appendectomy, C-section, abdominal wall surgery)
Component of multimodal analgesia in enhanced-recovery pathways
landmarkTechnique: Historic "double-pop" landmark technique feels two fascial clicks (external oblique/internal oblique, then internal oblique/transversus abdominis) at the lumbar triangle of Petit; largely superseded by ultrasound guidance for accuracy.
ultrasoundApproach: Probe placed transversely on the anterolateral abdominal wall between the costal margin and iliac crest; three muscle layers (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis) are identified, with the target plane being the fascial layer between internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
needleApproach: In-plane, depositing local anesthetic within the TAP, watching for fluid spread separating the two muscle layers.
keyComplications: Intraperitoneal injection/visceral injury (rare with ultrasound guidance)
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity given bilateral large-volume dosing — see LAST crisis algorithm
Transient femoral nerve weakness if spread tracks inferiorly (uncommon)
pearls: Provides somatic (skin/muscle) analgesia only — does not cover visceral pain, so it is an adjunct within multimodal analgesia, not a stand-alone anesthetic
Calculate total planned local anesthetic dose carefully when blocking bilaterally — see the LA maximum dose calculator

source.title: Widely-taught regional anesthesia technique structure (textbook-level, ASRA/NYSORA-style teaching descriptions)

name: Erector Spinae Plane (ESP) Block
targetNervesOrPlane: Dorsal and ventral rami of spinal nerves via spread deep to erector spinae muscle, craniocaudal along the paraspinal fascial plane
commonIndications: Thoracic and abdominal wall analgesia (rib fractures, thoracotomy/thoracoscopic surgery, abdominal surgery depending on level)
Increasingly used as a simpler, lower-risk alternative/adjunct to paravertebral or epidural blocks in some practices
patientPosition: Sitting, lateral, or prone depending on the level and operator preference
landmarkTechnique: Not typically performed by landmark alone — ultrasound guidance is standard given the need to identify the correct transverse process level and fascial plane.
ultrasoundApproach: Probe placed longitudinally (parasagittal) over the transverse process at the target vertebral level; the erector spinae muscle is identified overlying the transverse process, with the target plane being deep to the muscle and superficial to the transverse process.
needleApproach: In-plane, cephalad-to-caudad or caudad-to-cephalad, contacting the transverse process before withdrawing slightly to deposit local anesthetic in the correct plane.
keyComplications: Generally favorable safety profile given the plane's distance from pleura/neuraxis, though pneumothorax and epidural spread have been reported
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity given large volumes — see LAST crisis algorithm
contraindications: Coagulopathy (relative — though often considered lower-risk than neuraxial/paravertebral techniques)
pearls: Mechanism and reliability of spread are still an active area of study/debate in the literature — confirm current evidence and your unit's adopted indications before relying on it as a sole technique for major surgery
Contacting the transverse process (bony endpoint) before injecting is a key safety step distinguishing it from a paravertebral block

source.title: Widely-taught regional anesthesia technique structure (textbook-level, ASRA/NYSORA-style teaching descriptions)

name: Rectus Sheath Block
targetNervesOrPlane: Terminal branches of T9–T11 (sometimes T7/T8) intercostal nerves within the posterior rectus sheath
commonIndications: Midline abdominal incisions (umbilical hernia repair, laparoscopic port sites, midline laparotomy analgesia adjunct)
landmarkTechnique: Not typically performed by landmark alone given the need to visualize the posterior rectus sheath and avoid peritoneal puncture.
ultrasoundApproach: Probe placed transversely over the rectus abdominis muscle lateral to the umbilicus; the target plane is between the posterior rectus sheath and the rectus abdominis muscle, with the peritoneum visible just deep to the sheath.
needleApproach: In-plane, aiming to pierce the posterior sheath just enough to deposit local anesthetic in the plane without entering the peritoneal cavity.
keyComplications: Peritoneal puncture / visceral injury if the needle is advanced too deep
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity given bilateral dosing — see LAST crisis algorithm
pearls: Good adjunct specifically for midline incisions — does not cover lateral abdominal wall pain (pair with a TAP block if the incision extends laterally)

source.title: Widely-taught regional anesthesia technique structure (textbook-level, ASRA/NYSORA-style teaching descriptions)

name: Spinal (Subarachnoid) Block
targetNervesOrPlane: Spinal nerve roots within the subarachnoid space (CSF)
commonIndications: Lower abdominal, pelvic, and lower limb surgery
Cesarean section
Single-shot technique for procedures of predictable, limited duration
patientPosition: Sitting or lateral decubitus, with lumbar flexion ("arching the back") to open the interspinous spaces
landmarkTechnique: Midline or paramedian approach at L3-4 or L4-5 (below the conus medullaris, classically estimated using Tuffier's line at the level of the iliac crests), advancing through skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous/interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, and dura until free flow of CSF is obtained.
needleApproach: Midline or paramedian, typically with a pencil-point (atraumatic) needle to reduce post-dural-puncture headache risk.
localAnestheticVolume: 1–3 mL (dose is by total mg/baricity, not a volume-based teaching range like peripheral blocks — dosing depends heavily on patient height, desired block height, and drug baricity)
keyComplications: Hypotension/bradycardia from sympathetic blockade
High/total spinal (respiratory/cardiovascular collapse — requires immediate airway/hemodynamic support)
Post-dural-puncture headache
Rare: epidural hematoma, meningitis, transient neurologic symptoms
contraindications: Coagulopathy/anticoagulation per current neuraxial-anticoagulation timing guidance (verify against current ASRA-style interval tables before proceeding)
Local infection at the injection site
pearls: Confirm neuraxial anticoagulation timing intervals against current guidance for the specific agent before every block — these intervals are updated periodically and are not safe to recall from memory alone
Have vasopressors and IV fluids immediately available before performing the block given the predictable hemodynamic effects

source.title: Widely-taught regional anesthesia technique structure (textbook-level, ASRA/NYSORA-style teaching descriptions)

name: Epidural Block (incl. Labour Epidural)
targetNervesOrPlane: Spinal nerve roots via local anesthetic spread within the epidural space (outside the dura)
commonIndications: Labour analgesia
Post-operative analgesia (thoracic/abdominal surgery)
Surgical anesthesia (often combined with general anesthesia for major abdominal/thoracic cases)
patientPosition: Sitting or lateral decubitus, with lumbar (or thoracic, per indication) flexion
landmarkTechnique: Midline or paramedian approach using loss-of-resistance (to saline or air, per operator preference) as the needle passes through ligamentum flavum into the epidural space; a catheter is then threaded for continuous infusion or intermittent bolusing.
needleApproach: Midline or paramedian, Tuohy needle with loss-of-resistance technique; test dose given before full dosing to help exclude inadvertent intrathecal or intravascular placement.
localAnestheticVolume: Test dose 3–5 mL, then incremental/infusion dosing titrated to effect — total volumes vary widely by indication (labour vs. surgical vs. postoperative) and are not a single fixed range
keyComplications: Inadvertent dural puncture ("wet tap") and post-dural-puncture headache
Inadvertent intrathecal injection (high/total spinal) or intravascular injection (LAST) if the test dose is not respected
Epidural hematoma/abscess (rare but serious)
Hypotension from sympathetic blockade
contraindications: Coagulopathy/anticoagulation per current neuraxial-anticoagulation timing guidance
Local infection at the injection site
pearls: Always give and interpret a test dose (classically epinephrine-containing) before committing to the full epidural dose — a positive test dose (heart rate rise) suggests intravascular placement
Confirm neuraxial anticoagulation timing intervals against current guidance before catheter placement AND before removal — removal timing is just as important as insertion timing
